about: The rubrics call the sentence before Pater noster the preface of the Lord's Prayer. After et ne nos indúcas in tentatiónem, they assign the response sed líbera nos a malo to the server. The same words are also available here as a prayer on their own.

s03.translation: At the Saviour's command and formed by divine teaching, we dare to say:

s04.narrative: The priest spreads his hands, and keeps them so through the prayer.

s05.translation: Our Father, who art in heaven,

s08.translation: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

s09.translation: Give us this day our daily bread.

s10.translation: And forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.

s11.translation: And lead us not into temptation,

w004.function: A participle agreeing with the unexpressed nos, the subject of audémus.

w007.function: Ablative of means with formáti. Here institutio means instruction: formed by divine teaching.

w008.function: A participle agreeing with the unexpressed nos, the subject of audémus.

w009.function: “Audémus dícere” expresses filial boldness: instructed by Christ, we dare to say “Our Father.”

w011.function: Vocative singular in direct address to God.

w012.function: Vocative masculine singular agreeing with Pater.

w014.function: After the vocative the relative clause keeps the 2nd person: “who art”, not “who is”.

w016.function: Ablative plural after in. The received English renders it in the singular.

w017.function: Third-person present passive subjunctive expressing a petition.

w019.function: Nominative neuter singular agreeing with nomen.

w020.function: Optative subjunctive — the second petition: “may it come”.

w021.function: The subject of the petition: what is to come?

w023.function: The third petition: “may it be done”. The same “fiat” Mary answers with at the Annunciation (Lk 1:38).

w024.function: The subject of the petition: what is to be done?

w035.function: The first petition voiced as a direct imperative. The negative petition “indúcas” (w052) will use the subjunctive instead.

w040.function: Forgive for whom — for us: the person forgiven stands in the dative.

w043.function: Opens the comparison with our own forgiving.

w045.function: The subject spelled out for emphasis.

w046.function: Indicative — a statement of fact, not a petition: this is what we do.

w047.function: We forgive whom — the debtors. Literally “to the debtors”, traditionally “those who trespass against us”.

w050.function: With the subjunctive “indúcas” (w052) it forms a negative main petition: “do not…” — a direct prohibition, not a subordinate clause.

w052.function: Subjunctive after “ne” (w050) — the negation rides on “ne”. The received English joins them as “lead us not”.

w053.function: With the accusative — direction: “into temptation”. Compare “in” (w015) with the ablative — place.

w055.function: The server's voice begins here: the priest stopped at the colon, and the seventh petition is answered back to him.

w056.function: The word the prayer that follows will take up and expand — Líbera nos, quǽsumus, Dómine, ab ómnibus malis: the same imperative opening the embolism.

w059.function: The form leaves the gender open: neuter “malum” (evil) or masculine “malus” (the Evil One)? The tradition reads both senses at once, and the embolism just after the prayer takes the word up in the neuter plural — ab ómnibus malis.

w060.function: The priest's own: the page rubric has him say it secrete, the Ritus servandus submissa voce, in a lowered voice. The edition follows the page rubric and records the disagreement.
